items.readable_text:
Content:
The Fourier convergence theorem describes how a Fourier series behaves, especially at points where the original function is not continuous.

Content:
A Fourier series is built from smooth sine and cosine waves, so it cannot “jump” instantly the way a function with a jump discontinuity can. Instead, the series converges to an average value at these jumps.

Content:
More precisely, let [MATH: f(x)] be a [MATH: 2L]-periodic piecewise smooth function, and let its Fourier series be
[MATH: S(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(
a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)
\right).]
Then the Fourier series converges for every [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R}]. The value it converges to depends on whether [MATH: f] is continuous at [MATH: x].

Content:
- If [MATH: f(x)] is continuous at [MATH: x,] the series converges to the function value:
[MATH: S(x)=f(x)]
- If [MATH: f(x)] has a jump discontinuity at [MATH: x,] the series converges to the midpoint of the one-sided limits:
[MATH: S(x)=\dfrac{f^-(x)+f^+(x)}{2},]
where [MATH: f^-(x)] and [MATH: f^+(x)] are the left- and right-sided limits of [MATH: f] at [MATH: x,] respectively.

Content:
Let's see a concrete example.

items.title: Identifying the Value to What a Fourier Series Converges

sections.normalized_html: [MATH: {− 1,|x ∈ [− (π)/(2), 0]; 2,|x ∈ (0, (π)/(2))] Consider the function [MATH: F(x)] shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] converges when [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: {− 1,|x ∈ [− (π)/(2), 0]; 2,|x ∈ (0, (π)/(2))]
Consider the function [MATH: F(x)] shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] converges when [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x)] is a [MATH: 2L]-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series [MATH: S(x) = \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg).] Then, the series converges for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}.]

  • If [MATH: f(x)] is continuous at [MATH: x,] then the series converges to the value of the function at this point: [MATH: S(x) = f(x)]

  • If [MATH: f(x)] has a jump discontinuity at [MATH: x,] then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point: [MATH: S(x) = \dfrac{f^-(x)+f^+(x)}{2}] where [MATH: f^-(x)] and [MATH: f^-(x)] are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of our function [MATH: F(x)] is not continuous at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.] The one-sided limits at this point are the following: [MATH: f^{−}((π)/(2))|= lim_(x → (π/2)^{−})f(x) = 2; f^{+}((π)/(2))|= lim_(x → (π/2)^{+})f(x) = − 1]

Therefore, the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] converges to [MATH: \dfrac{f^-\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+f^+\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}{2} = \dfrac{2+(-1)}{2} = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{2}}.]

Content:
A powerful application of Fourier series is evaluating infinite sums. The strategy is to find a known Fourier series that contains the sum we want, and then choose a convenient value of [MATH: x] to plug in.

Content:
For example, consider the function [MATH: F(x)=x^2] defined on [MATH: x \in [-\pi,\pi).] The Fourier series of the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} \cos(nx).]
Let's use this to find the value of the infinite sum [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2}.]

Content:
Now, notice that at [MATH: x=0,] we have
[MATH: \cos\left(n\cdot0\right) = \cos\left(0\right) = 1.]

Content:
By the pointwise convergence theorem, since [MATH: f(x)] is continuous at [MATH: x=0,] the corresponding Fourier series converges to
[MATH: f\left(0\right) = 0.]

Content:
Hence, we have the following equation:
[MATH: f(0)|= (π^{2})/(3) + 4∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}) ⋅ \cos (n ⋅ 0); 0|= (π^{2})/(3) + 4∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}) ⋅ 1; − (π^{2})/(3)|= 4∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}); − (π^{2})/(12)|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2})]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -\dfrac{\pi^2}{12}.]

items.title: Finding the Value of an Infinite Sum Using Fourier Series

sections.normalized_html: [MATH: {− 1,|x ∈ [− π, 0]; 1,|x ∈ (0, π)] Consider the function [MATH: F(x)] shown above. The Fourier series of the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] is given by [MATH: f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)} \sin((2n-1)x).] Use this Fourier series to find the sum of the series [MATH: \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}.]
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: {− 1,|x ∈ [− π, 0]; 1,|x ∈ (0, π)]
Consider the function [MATH: F(x)] shown above. The Fourier series of the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)} \sin((2n-1)x).]
Use this Fourier series to find the sum of the series
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we notice that at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] we have [MATH: \sin\left((2n-1)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}+n\pi\right) = (-1)^{n+1}.]

So, substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] into the given Fourier series gives [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)} \sin\left((2n-1)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)}(-1)^{n+1}.]

Content:
Even though the Fourier series converges to the correct value at each point (using the midpoint rule at jumps), the graphs of the partial sums can behave strangely near a jump discontinuity.

Content:
Suppose [MATH: f(x)] has a jump discontinuity at [MATH: x=x_0]. Then:

Content:
- The Fourier series converges at the jump to the midpoint:
[MATH: S(x_0)=\dfrac{f^-(x_0)+f^+(x_0)}{2}.]
- However, for large [MATH: N], the partial sum
[MATH: S_N(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(
a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)
\right)]
typically overshoots above the higher side of the jump and undershoots below the lower side.

Content:
As [MATH: N] increases, the oscillations get squeezed into a smaller neighborhood around [MATH: x_0], but the size of the overshoot does not go to [MATH: 0]. This persistent overshoot near jump discontinuities is called the Gibbs phenomenon.

Content:
For example, for the Fourier series of the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of the function [MATH: F(x)=x,] defined on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi),] the phenomenon can be observed at each point of discontinuity on the graph below.

Graphic:

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The Fourier convergence theorem describes how a Fourier series behaves, especially at points where the original function is not continuous.

Content:
A Fourier series is built from smooth sine and cosine waves, so it cannot “jump” instantly the way a function with a jump discontinuity can. Instead, the series converges to an average value at these jumps.

Content:
More precisely, let [MATH: f(x)] be a [MATH: 2L]-periodic piecewise smooth function, and let its Fourier series be
[MATH: S(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(
a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)
\right).]
Then the Fourier series converges for every [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R}]. The value it converges to depends on whether [MATH: f] is continuous at [MATH: x].

Content:
- If [MATH: f(x)] is continuous at [MATH: x,] the series converges to the function value:
[MATH: S(x)=f(x)]
- If [MATH: f(x)] has a jump discontinuity at [MATH: x,] the series converges to the midpoint of the one-sided limits:
[MATH: S(x)=\dfrac{f^-(x)+f^+(x)}{2},]
where [MATH: f^-(x)] and [MATH: f^+(x)] are the left- and right-sided limits of [MATH: f] at [MATH: x,] respectively.

Content:
Let's see a concrete example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: An Example of Approximation

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: F(x)=x] defined on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi).] The Fourier series of its [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) \sim S(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin\left(nx\right).]
The graph of the function [MATH: y=f(x)] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/438329a0964a79faee72543b791dabba]

Content:
We can approximate the function [MATH: f(x)] by summing a finite number of terms from its Fourier series. These approximations are called partial sums:
[MATH: S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\dfrac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin\left(nx\right)]
As [MATH: N] increases, the partial sums match the graph of [MATH: f(x)] more closely.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4e830c11abf24b1681fd29baaef91a66]

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: An Example of Convergence

Content:
As we saw, the partial sums [MATH: S_N(x)] appear to converge to the function [MATH: f(x)] as [MATH: N\to\infty]. The Fourier convergence theorem specifies the exact value to which the series converges.

Content:
- At any point [MATH: x_0] where [MATH: f(x)] is continuous, the Fourier series converges to the function value:
[MATH: S(x_0)=f(x_0)]
- At any point [MATH: x_0] where [MATH: f(x)] has a jump discontinuity, the Fourier series converges to the midpoint of the jump (the average of the one-sided limits):
[MATH: S(x_0)=\dfrac{f^-(x_0)+f^+(x_0)}{2}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b503427dcb5c97b8d42ab5ba66bbcd70]

Content:
For our sawtooth function above, the discontinuities occur at [MATH: x=(2k+1)\pi]. At [MATH: x=\pi], for example, the series converges to:
[MATH: S(\pi)=\dfrac{f^-(\pi)+f^+(\pi)}{2} = \dfrac{\pi + (-\pi)}{2} = 0]
The graph of the limit function [MATH: S(x)] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c96e42957c5a8441a9e0d906e1128889]

Content:
Note: The limit function [MATH: S(x)] is the same as [MATH: f(x)] except at the jump discontinuities. If [MATH: f(x)] were continuous everywhere, then its Fourier series would converge to [MATH: f(x)] at every point, and we could write [MATH: f(x)=S(x)] instead of [MATH: f(x)\sim S(x)].

---

Item 4 — Example: Identifying the Value to What a Fourier Series Converges

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {− 1,|x ∈ [− (π)/(2), 0]; 2,|x ∈ (0, (π)/(2))]
Consider the function [MATH: F(x)] shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] converges when [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x)] is a [MATH: 2L]-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series
[MATH: S(x) = \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg).]
Then, the series converges for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}.]

- If [MATH: f(x)] is continuous at [MATH: x,] then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:
[MATH: S(x) = f(x)]
- If [MATH: f(x)] has a jump discontinuity at [MATH: x,] then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:
[MATH: S(x) = \dfrac{f^-(x)+f^+(x)}{2}]
where [MATH: f^-(x)] and [MATH: f^-(x)] are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of our function [MATH: F(x)] is not continuous at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.] The one-sided limits at this point are the following:
[MATH: f^{−}((π)/(2))|= lim_(x → (π/2)^{−})f(x) = 2; f^{+}((π)/(2))|= lim_(x → (π/2)^{+})f(x) = − 1]

Therefore, the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] converges to
[MATH: \dfrac{f^-\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+f^+\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}{2} = \dfrac{2+(-1)}{2} = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{2}}.]

---

Item 7 — Tutorial: Using Fourier Series For Finding Infinite Sums

Content:
A powerful application of Fourier series is evaluating infinite sums. The strategy is to find a known Fourier series that contains the sum we want, and then choose a convenient value of [MATH: x] to plug in.

Content:
For example, consider the function [MATH: F(x)=x^2] defined on [MATH: x \in [-\pi,\pi).] The Fourier series of the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} \cos(nx).]
Let's use this to find the value of the infinite sum [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2}.]

Content:
Now, notice that at [MATH: x=0,] we have
[MATH: \cos\left(n\cdot0\right) = \cos\left(0\right) = 1.]

Content:
By the pointwise convergence theorem, since [MATH: f(x)] is continuous at [MATH: x=0,] the corresponding Fourier series converges to
[MATH: f\left(0\right) = 0.]

Content:
Hence, we have the following equation:
[MATH: f(0)|= (π^{2})/(3) + 4∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}) ⋅ \cos (n ⋅ 0); 0|= (π^{2})/(3) + 4∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}) ⋅ 1; − (π^{2})/(3)|= 4∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}); − (π^{2})/(12)|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n})/(n^{2})]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -\dfrac{\pi^2}{12}.]

---

Item 8 — Example: Finding the Value of an Infinite Sum Using Fourier Series

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {− 1,|x ∈ [− π, 0]; 1,|x ∈ (0, π)]
Consider the function [MATH: F(x)] shown above. The Fourier series of the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)} \sin((2n-1)x).]
Use this Fourier series to find the sum of the series
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we notice that at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] we have
[MATH: \sin\left((2n-1)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}+n\pi\right) = (-1)^{n+1}.]

So, substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] into the given Fourier series gives
[MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)} \sin\left((2n-1)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)
= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{4}{\pi(2n-1)}(-1)^{n+1}.]

Next, since [MATH: f(x)] is continuous at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] the Fourier series converges to [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \in [0,\pi),] we have
[MATH: f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1.]

Therefore,
[MATH: 1|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(4)/(π(2n − 1))(− 1)^{n + 1}; (π)/(4)|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n + 1})/(2n − 1).]

So, we conclude that
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}.]

Content:

Content:
Suppose [MATH: f(x)] has a jump discontinuity at [MATH: x=x_0]. Then:

[MATH: S(x_0)=\dfrac{f^-(x_0)+f^+(x_0)}{2}.]

[MATH: S_N(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(
a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)
\right)]
